name: Nurse
summary: Nurse interviews usually test clinical judgement and patient safety as much as knowledge: candidates commonly report scenario questions on a patient who is getting worse, medication safety, prioritising a busy shift and escalating concerns, plus questions on teamwork and communicating with patients and families. For nursing jobs abroad, values-based interviews are common with many employers, for example in the UK.
rounds: Application and document check: qualifications, experience and registration
Written or skills test on nursing basics at some hospitals
Interview with the nursing superintendent, ward manager or a panel: clinical scenarios and experience
Values-based interview, common for many jobs abroad
Practical skills check for some roles
HR round on shifts, joining and documents
looks_for: Patient safety first: identity checks, medication safety, infection control
Recognising a deteriorating patient and escalating promptly
Prioritising care when several patients need you at once
Clear, kind communication with patients and families
Honesty about mistakes and working within your scope of practice

questions.text: Tell me about a time you noticed a patient getting worse. What did you do?
covers: What you noticed: observations, behaviour, what the patient said
Who you told, how quickly, and how you passed on the facts clearly
What happened next and what you learned

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made or spotted a mistake in patient care. How was it handled?
covers: The mistake in plain words, owned honestly
Making the patient safe and reporting it the way your hospital requires
What changed so it wouldn't happen again

questions.text: Describe a time you supported a distressed patient or family member.
covers: What was upsetting them
How you listened, explained and comforted them
Any help you brought in, such as a doctor or counsellor

questions.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a colleague or doctor about a patient's care.
covers: Your concern and why it mattered for the patient
How you raised it respectfully, and escalated if needed
The outcome and how you worked together afterwards

questions.text: Tell me about a very busy shift. How did you decide what to do first?
covers: What made it busy
How you prioritised and who you asked for help
What you'd do the same or differently

questions.text: You're caring for several patients and two need you at the same moment. How do you decide who comes first?
covers: Assessing who is most at risk, with airway, breathing and circulation first
Asking for help or handing over tasks others can do safely
Telling the waiting patient, and documenting what you did

questions.text: What checks do you make before giving any medication?
covers: Confirming the patient's identity and allergies
Checking the prescription: drug, dose, route, time and that it's due
Stopping to clarify anything unclear, and documenting after giving it

questions.text: How do you help prevent infection spreading on a ward?
covers: Hand hygiene at the right moments
Protective equipment and isolation when needed
Cleaning, safe disposal of sharps and waste, and following local policy

questions.text: What would you include in a handover at the end of your shift?
covers: A structured format such as SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation
Changes, pending tasks, risks and anything the next nurse must watch
Checking the other nurse has understood

questions.text: A patient refuses a treatment the doctor has prescribed. What would you do?
covers: Finding out why, and explaining the treatment in simple words
Respecting their right to decide when they are able to make the decision
Informing the doctor and documenting the conversation

questions.text: A relative is angry about how long their family member has been waiting. How would you handle it?
covers: Listening calmly and acknowledging their worry
Explaining what's happening, honestly, and checking on the patient
Involving the nurse in charge if it escalates

questions.text: How would you care for a patient who doesn't speak your language?
covers: Using a trained interpreter or approved service, rather than relying on family where possible
Simple words, pictures and checking understanding
Respecting their culture and documenting how you communicated

questions.text: You think a colleague has come to work in a state where they can't care for patients safely. What would you do?
covers: Putting patient safety first
Raising it promptly with the nurse in charge or your manager
Following the hospital's policy rather than ignoring it or handling it alone

questions.text: What does dignity in care mean to you, and how do you show it during routine tasks?
covers: Privacy, consent and explaining before you act
Involving patients in decisions about their care
A specific example, such as personal care or a ward round

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and your clinical experience.
covers: Your qualification and registration status
The wards, units or postings you've worked in
What kind of nursing you want to do next
A personal reason, shown by an experience
What you value in the work
How that shows in the way you care for patients

questions.text: Why this hospital or unit? If you're applying abroad, why that country?
covers: Specific things about the hospital, unit or employer, such as its specialities or published values
How your experience fits
For abroad: realistic reasons and preparation for working there

questions.text: How do you look after yourself after a hard shift?
covers: Honest, healthy ways you recover
Using support from colleagues or supervisors after difficult events
Why it matters for patient care

tips: Answer clinical scenarios in order: keep the patient safe, assess, escalate to the right person, then document.
Name the structured approaches you were taught, such as ABCDE assessment or SBAR handover, and explain them in plain words.
Freshers: prepare examples from your clinical postings and internship.
For jobs abroad, read the employer's published values and prepare a short example for each; values-based interviews commonly ask for them.
Never guess a drug dose or clinical fact in an interview; say how you'd check it, such as with the prescriber, a pharmacist or a protocol.
Keep your registration, certificates and experience letters in order; some employers check them early.
